Physical computing connects a program to the world. A small computer reads an input, makes a decision, and controls an output. The exact board may change, but the same ideas apply to Arduino-compatible boards, micro:bit, Raspberry Pi, and other controllers.

## Build the foundation

::: {.ter-path-grid}
::: {.ter-path-card}
### Stable inputs

Learn logic levels, switches, pull-up and pull-down resistors, active-low signals, and debouncing before connecting an input pin.

[Open Digital Logic](../03-digital-logic-inputs/index.qmd)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### Programming ideas

Use variables, conditions, loops, functions, and state machines to turn a process into code.

[Explore algorithms and state machines](../engineering-preparation-track/index.qmd#boolean-logic-algorithms-and-state-machines)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### Sensors and outputs

Read a sensor, check its range and units, then control an LED, motor, relay, display, or another useful output.

[Explore sensors and measurement](../engineering-preparation-track/index.qmd#sensors-and-measurement)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### Build a system

Combine an input, decision, output, test plan, and clear explanation in a small project.

[Open the sensor, logic, and actuator project](../engineering-preparation-track/index.qmd#sensor-logic-and-actuator-project)
:::
:::

Always check the exact board voltage, pin limits, component polarity, and required protection. Don't assume every controller uses the same electrical levels.
